Learning Objectives
Review the populations at high risk for a stress fracture and the clinical signs of a stress
fracture.
Describe the mechanisms of injury that lead to a stress fracture.
Discuss the classification of stress fractures and the radiologic and clinical features used in
their characterization.
Explain the evaluation of stress fractures.
Define various aspects of a treatment plan and relate those aspects of management to the
causative mechanisms of stress fracture.

Stress fractures are common in highly committed athletes and tend to occur in sports that
involve repetitive, high-impact weight-bearing activity. They are the most severe response as
part of the continuum of bone stress injuries.
Stress fractures and stress reactions occur if repetitive microtrauma to a bone exceeds the
capacity of the bone to withstand and repair from the microtrauma.
Stress fractures are uncommon in the ribs and the upper extremities but occur with upper
extremity weight-bearing and repetitive tasks.
Most bony stress injuries occur in the lower extremity, with the tibia and metatarsals being the
most common locations.
Stress fractures occur in less than 1% of the general athletic population; however, the
incidence in running/track athletes may be as high as 10% to 20%. The rate of recurrence may
be approximately 10% in all athletes but as high as 50% in runners.
Populations at greatest risk for stress fractures include women with the female athlete triad
(disordered eating, amenorrhea, and osteoporosis) and those with vitamin D insufficiency. A
body mass index of less than 19 kg/m2 is a risk factor for stress fracture and extended time to
return to sports activity.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Stress fracture is a fatigue failure of bone that occurs in three stages: crack initiation, crack
propagation, and final fracture.
Stress fractures represent a continuum of severity of bone injury (Table 1); they result from
accumulation of microdamage that occurs with repetitive loading. The area of initial stress
concentration is termed crack initiation.
If the initial microscopic crack is not repaired and repeated loading of the bone continues, the
crack extends and is referred to as crack propagation, eventually resulting in a final fracture.
In vivo, bone responds to crack initiation and propagation with a reparative biologic response
that is dependent on age, nutritional status, hormone status, vascular supply, biomechanical
factors, and possibly genetic predisposition.
A dynamic balance exists between the accumulation of microdamage and the host repair
processes.
If microdamage accumulation exceeds the reparative response, the result is a stress fracture.
Any factor that disrupts this dynamic balance can increase the risk of stress fracture.
Any factor that increases tensile, compressive, or torsional forces on a bone may cause an
increase in microdamage accumulation with each loading episode, especially if applied with

Injury Classification
Stress fractures generally are classified as low risk or high risk, depending on the location;
those with a poor natural history are deemed high risk (Table 2) and usually require aggressive
management.
Delayed recognition or undermanagement of high-risk stress fractures tends to result in
fracture progression, nonunion, the need for surgical management, refracture, and delayed
return to sports activity.

Other fractures have a more benign natural history and are low-risk stress fractures; these
fractures tend to heal with activity modifications because of compressive forces and adequate
vascularity.
Recognizing the class of stress fracture is important for optimizing management.
Over-management of a low-risk stress fracture or undermanagement of a high-risk fracture
may result in undue loss of playing time, deconditioning, and prolonged recovery.
MRI classification of stress fractures has been correlated with time to return to play (Table 3).
A recent generalizable clinical and radiologic classification system has been shown to be
associated with high intraobserver and interobserver reliability for grading stress fractures
(Table 4).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Stress fractures typically present as an insidious onset of pain but may present as an acute
onset of pain with or without prodromal pain for weeks to months.
A history of prolonged high-impact activity or a recent abrupt increase in training frequency or
intensity usually is noted. Alternatively, a recent change in the type of training (eg, introduction
of interval training) or equipment (eg, a new brand of shoes) may have occurred.

With no history of substantial repetitive loading episodes, an insufficiency fracture or
pathologic fracture must be considered, especially in patients with decreased bone density,
inadequate nutrition, or abnormal bone quality.
Physical Examination
Physical examination may reveal pain with direct palpation or mechanical loading of the
affected site, with fulcrum testing of long bones and single-leg hop testing.
Imaging Studies
Radiography, bone scintigraphy, CT, and MRI are the imaging modalities used to evaluate
stress fractures. Each imaging modality is associated with advantages and disadvantages, with
MRI being the preferred imaging modality because of its high sensitivity and specificity.
Radiography
Radiographs are rarely positive unless the injury is severe or chronic. Typically, radiographic
findings lag behind clinical symptoms for weeks to months.
Computed Tomography
Identifying the presence of a nonunion and assessing the amount of healing in preparation for
possible surgical management is best achieved via CT; however, this imaging modality is
associated with a substantial radiation dose.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can identify the bony edema associated with early stress concentration or reveal the
presence of a fracture line (Table 3).
MRI is advantageous because it shows the surrounding soft tissues and is most predictive of
time to return to athletic activity.
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy is a relatively inexpensive, widely available, and quick diagnostic imaging
modality performed with technetium-99m–labeled diphosphonates.

In athletes, bone scintigraphy can be performed to differentiate tibial stress fractures from
shin splints.1
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography has been described for the imaging of stress fractures but is used much less
commonly because of its inability to penetrate the cortex.
Ultrasonography is advantageous because no ionizing radiation is involved and a focused, real-
time evaluation of the fracture can be performed.
Positron Emission Tomography
Combined positron emission tomography/MRI is just beginning to be used; this imaging
modality combines the ability to observe metabolic activity via positron emission tomography
scans with the soft-tissue imaging of MRI.
In several small clinical series, patients with a stress fracture of the foot were diagnosed
despite negative radiographs.2
Although potentially promising, positron emission tomography/MRI is still in the experimental
stages.
Other Studies
Bone scans are very sensitive in identifying the presence and location of stress fractures;
however, but they do not reveal macroscopic fracture lines in the bone and may remain
positive for as long as 2 years after the injury is clinically healed.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Treatment Principles
Management must alter the biomechanical and biologic environment to allow the reparative
processes to overcome the accumulation of microdamage at the fracture site. A holistic
approach is required to optimize healing potential.

An athlete’s biologic bone-healing capacity should be evaluated. This includes a review of
nutritional, hormonal, psychological, biomechanical, and medication status.
The female athlete triad (amenorrhea, disordered eating, and osteoporosis) must be
considered in any female athlete with a stress fracture; appropriate evaluation and
management should be initiated.
The fracture site also must be protected from future strain episodes via relative rest, absolute
rest, bracing management, technique modifications, or surgical fixation (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Treatment algorithm for the management of stress fractures based on injury severity
according to the Kaeding-Miller classification system. (Reproduced with permission from
Tornetta P III, Ricci WM, Ostrum RF, McQueen MM, McKee MD, Court-Brown CM, eds:
Rockwood and Green’s Fractures in Adults, ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Wolters Kluwer, 2019.)

Relative rest involves decreasing the frequency or magnitude of strain episodes at the stress
fracture site by modifying the training volume (intensity, duration, and frequency), technique,
and equipment; using a brace or orthosis; or by cross-training.
Absolute rest removes all strain episodes from the fracture site. This often is achieved by
having the athlete bear no weight, use crutches, and undergo immobilization.
An assessment of biomechanical risk factors, such as malalignment, should be performed to
assess the likelihood of recurrence. Video running gait analysis and throwing analysis are ideal
for determining form and technique abnormalities.
The use of biophysical enhancement technologies in stress fractures, such as pulsed
ultrasonography and electrical stimulation, is not a major factor in healing an acute stress
injury.
Nutritional support with appropriate caloric intake along with calcium and vitamin D
supplementation are required to achieve healing and prevent recurrence. Nutritional
laboratory values may be required in athletes with multiple or recurrent bony stress injuries.
Given these principles, the management of stress fractures depends on classifying each
fracture as high or minimal risk (Figure 1).
High-risk stress fractures typically are managed via absolute rest or surgery (Figure 2).
The level of risk for catastrophic injury must be seriously considered before allowing patients
with a high-risk stress fracture to continue to play; however, patients with a low-risk stress
fracture may continue to play with activity modifications/relative rest (Figure 3).

Surgical Management

Surgical Management
In evaluating a stress injury of the anterior tibia, the level of very high risk of progression
to a complete fracture should be based on the presence of the dreaded black line on the
anterior tibia cortex on radiographs. Additional association with a moderate degree of
pain should be considered an additional warning sign of the progression to complete
fracture. Surgical stabilization should be considered for such fractures. Posteromedial
stress fractures on the compression side of the tibia may have a similar association with
pain; however, they are not associated with the dreaded black line, are not candidates
